label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
output:
Here's a draft. I kept the old gentleman vague (no "three days", no ward or time), and I wasn't sure whether you'd already started days by the time you post, so check the Monday line.

---

**Last night shift**

It's been a while. Longer than I meant, and I'll skip the apology. I've started this post several times since spring and each attempt turned into either a eulogy or a rant about the NHS. I've written enough of the second, and I'm not dead, and neither are nights, so I'm going to try and just say what happened.

On Saturday I worked my last night shift. 21:00 to 07:30, majors. After fourteen years, from Monday I'm on the days-only rota.

I asked for this, or at least I agreed to it. My knees have opinions now, my sleep is a rumour, and my GP told me, in the tone GPs use when they've decided you're not listening, that my blood pressure is no longer a joke. So it's the right decision. I'd tell anyone else in my position to take it. I'd also tell them to stop apologising for it, which is advice I'm not currently following.

Because I am relieved, and I feel like a traitor for being relieved. I keep waiting for one feeling to win and neither will.

**What nights gave me**

My first night shift as an SHO was in 2012. The first winter, I cried in the car park at the Infirmary at some miserable hour because I couldn't remember whether I'd given the second dose of something. I had. I'd checked the chart, and then I checked it again, and I still sat in the car with the engine off, shaking, with frost creeping across the windscreen. I remember the frost more clearly than I remember the drug. Nobody saw me, and I wiped my face and went back in.

I think about that car park more than I expected to this week. That version of me thought the job was getting everything right. Nights taught me that it's mostly about carrying on after you've worried you got something wrong, and checking, and asking someone, and being the sort of doctor who asks.

Nights are where the department is most itself. There are fewer managers and fewer meetings about the thing that happened, and almost nobody is performing. People say what they mean. If you're drowning, someone notices and takes a patient off you without being asked, and nobody mentions it afterwards. I've seen more ordinary kindness between 2am and 5am than I've seen in the whole of the daytime put together. Maybe days have it too and I've just never been there to see it. We'll find out.

People assume nights are about adrenaline, and some of it is. But mostly it's about staying kind at 5am when you're completely empty. When the department is full and the corridor is full and you've said the same sentence to nine different people, and the tenth person asks you the same thing again and deserves the same patience as the first. Nobody tells you that's the skill, and nobody can teach it. You learn it slowly, and it costs something every time.

Last winter, in the small hours, an older man in my care held my hand and told me I had his daughter's hands. I said thank you, because what else do you say. He went home a few days later. I don't know what became of him after that, and that's the deal with this job. You get a few hours with someone at their most frightened, and then you don't. I'm not sure that sentence belongs in a post about my rota, but it's the one that came to mind when I tried to work out what I'd actually miss.

**What nights took**

The list is the obvious one. Knees, sleep, blood pressure. A lot of daylight.

And my sister's family. I missed both of my nieces' naming ceremonies, and I watched them over video, because I was either about to go in to work or had just come out of it and was no use to anyone. My sister has never once complained. Not once, not even a pointed silence. She reads this blog, so: you know what that meant, and I'm not going to embarrass us both by saying it any louder. I'm sorry. Thank you. Both are true.

I don't want to turn that into a neat trade-off, though, because it isn't one. I didn't give those things up for something noble. I gave them up because that was the rota, and I was good at nights, and nights needed people. Both of those things can be true and still leave a gap where the ceremonies should have been.

**The drive home**

On Sunday morning I drove home down the London Road with the sun coming up. I had the shipping forecast on catch-up, which I've done for years because it's the only thing that gets my brain to stop replaying the shift. Dogger, Humber, Thames, someone reading out the weather for places I'll never see, and the light coming up pink and orange over the roofs.

Somewhere around the lights I realised I wouldn't see that light from that side again. I'll see sunrise, obviously, because I'll be asleep in the dark like a normal person, or I'll be getting up for it. But not like that, not with a whole night behind me and my hands still humming, feeling that strange mix of wrecked and awake and oddly grateful. That tiredness was a particular kind. I'd stopped noticing I liked it until I knew it was going.

I did not cry in the car this time. I'd like that noted. I did go a bit quiet on the A-road.

**Folasade**

Our charge nurse on nights, Folasade, has done nights for twenty-two years, and she still beats me up the stairs. I'm forty-two and I have the knees to prove I'm not keeping up. I've watched her run that department at its worst hours for most of my time there, and I don't think I've ever properly told her what that's been like to work beside. I'm not going to do it in a blog post either, but I'll say it to her face this week, and she'll wave it away, and that will be fine.

**The toast**

Someone always makes toast in the staff room at four in the morning. Nobody admits to starting it. I have worked fourteen years of nights and I still couldn't tell you who it is. You walk in and the smell is already there, and there's a plate going round, and someone's found the butter, and for ten minutes nobody is a consultant or a nurse or a registrar, we're just people eating toast at an hour when nothing else is normal.

I've decided not to investigate. I think the mystery is part of it.

On Saturday night, and every night after, the department will fill up, and the staffing will be what it is, and at some point around four someone will quietly put bread in the toaster. And nobody will admit to it, and everyone will eat it. I won't be there, and the place will be fine.

---

That comes to roughly 1,200 words. Things you may want to change: the "Monday" tense, whether you actually plan to tell Folasade in person (I wrote it that way, so cut it if not), and the "I did not cry in the car this time" line, which I added as a callback and is yours to keep or drop.
